extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning linear systems / dynamical systems
extracted.subtask_description: Provide methods and criteria to analyze, solve, and classify planar linear systems X' = AX via eigenvalues/eigenvectors, canonical forms, phase portraits, and the trace–determinant plane; determine qualitative behavior (saddle, sink, source, center, spirals) and construct solutions. Suitable for solving exercises and sketching phase portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real distinct eigenvalues classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When A has two real eigenvalues λ1 < λ2 (assume none equal to 0) there are three subcases: (1) λ1 < 0 < λ2, (2) λ1 < λ2 < 0, (3) 0 < λ1 < λ2. These correspond to qualitatively different phase portraits (saddle, sink, source).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General solution: X(t) = α e^{λ1 t} v1 + β e^{λ2 t} v2 where v1,v2 are eigenvectors. If λ1 < 0 < λ2, the x-axis/y-axis (eigenvector directions) are stable/unstable lines and the equilibrium is a saddle; typical solutions approach the unstable line as t→∞ and the stable line as t→−∞. If λ1<λ2<0, all solutions tend to origin (sink); define stronger (more negative) and weaker eigenvalue: solutions tend tangentially to the eigenvector of the weaker eigenvalue as t→∞. If 0<λ1<λ2, reverse time (source). Use slope dy/dx asymptotics to see tangency behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex eigenvalues classification (centers and spirals)
rubrics_metrics.description: If eigenvalues are complex α ± iβ (β ≠ 0), solutions are not straight lines; behavior depends on real part α: α = 0 gives a center (periodic orbits), α < 0 gives a spiral sink, α > 0 gives a spiral source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute complex eigenvector and use Euler's formula to obtain two real solutions X_re(t), X_im(t); general real solution is X(t)=c1 X_re(t)+c2 X_im(t). For α=0 solutions lie on circles of period 2π/β; for α≠0 solutions are e^{α t} times rotating sin/cos factors so trajectories spiral in/out. Direction of rotation is determined by sign of β (clockwise if β>0, counterclockwise if β<0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated eigenvalues cases and Jordan block behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: When A has a repeated real eigenvalue λ, two possibilities arise: (a) A is diagonalizable (two independent eigenvectors) — then A=λ I and every nonzero vector is an eigenvector so solutions are straight lines e^{λ t}V; (b) A has a single eigenvector (defective) and is similar to the Jordan block [λ 1; 0 λ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the defective case solutions take the form X(t) = α e^{λ t} [1;0] + β (e^{λ t} [t;1]) (i.e. terms with t e^{λ t}). If λ<0 all solutions →0, if λ>0 all →∞; solutions approach or depart tangent to the eigenvector direction. Construct generalized eigenvector U with (A−λI)U = V to build change-of-basis T producing canonical Jordan form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three canonical forms for 2×2 linear systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Any 2×2 matrix can be put (by change of coordinates) into one of three canonical forms: (i) diagonal form [λ 0; 0 μ] (real distinct eigenvalues), (ii) rotation/spiral form [α β; −β α] (complex eigenvalues α ± iβ), (iii) Jordan block [λ 1; 0 λ] (repeated eigenvalue with single eigenvector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put A into canonical form by finding an invertible T (columns chosen as eigenvectors or real/imag parts); then Y' = (T^{-1} A T) Y is the canonical system which is easy to solve and whose phase portrait maps via T to that of the original system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change-of-coordinates and invertibility condition
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear change of variables X = T Y converts X' = A X into Y' = (T^{-1} A T) Y. The matrix T must be invertible; T is invertible iff det T ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose T with columns equal to (independent) eigenvectors V1,V2 or with columns equal to the real and imaginary parts of a complex eigenvector. Compute S = T^{-1} = (1/det T) [d −b; −c a] when det T ≠ 0. Conjugacy via T maps solutions and phase portraits between systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace–determinant (T–D) classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize eigenvalues and qualitative behavior using trace T = tr A and determinant D = det A: eigenvalues are λ± = (1/2)(T ± sqrt(T^2 − 4D)). The sign of Δ = T^2 − 4D determines real vs complex roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If T^2 − 4D < 0 → complex eigenvalues: spiral sink if T<0, spiral source if T>0, center if T=0. If T^2 − 4D > 0 → real distinct eigenvalues: if D<0 → saddle; if D>0 and T<0 → real sink; if D>0 and T>0 → real source. If D=0 → at least one zero eigenvalue. Plotting (T,D) in TD-plane partitions system types; crossing parabola T^2−4D=0 or axes corresponds to bifurcations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase portrait vocabulary and qualitative features
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard qualitative types: saddle (one positive, one negative eigenvalue), sink (all eigenvalues negative), source (all positive), center (pure imaginary eigenvalues), spiral sink/source (complex eigenvalues with negative/positive real part). Also stable and unstable lines/manifolds corresponding to eigenvector directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable line: eigenvector direction with negative eigenvalue (solutions approach origin as t→∞). Unstable line: eigenvector with positive eigenvalue (solutions depart as t→∞). 'Stronger' and 'weaker' eigenvalues: solutions align with the weaker eigenvector as t→∞ (if magnitudes differ). Use slope dy/dx computations to determine tangency behavior near origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing real solutions from complex eigenpairs
rubrics_metrics.description: If λ = α + iβ is an eigenvalue with complex eigenvector V = V1 + i V2, then the real and imaginary parts X_re(t), X_im(t) of e^{(α+iβ)t}V provide two real linearly independent solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly X_re(t) = e^{α t}[cos βt V1 − sin βt V2], X_im(t) = e^{α t}[sin βt V1 + cos βt V2] (up to sign conventions). Their linear combinations give the general real solution. Use these to identify periods (2π/β) and spiral factors e^{α t}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solving linear systems via eigen-decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: compute eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors; assemble T whose columns are eigenvectors (or real/imag parts); then T^{-1} A T is canonical and solutions of Y'=(T^{-1}AT)Y give solutions X= T Y of the original system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many cases one can write down the general solution immediately as linear combinations of e^{λ t} times eigenvectors without forming T explicitly. For defective cases include t e^{λ t} terms (method of undetermined coefficients / generalized eigenvectors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of harmonic oscillator (second-order) systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A second-order oscillator x'' + b x' + k x = 0 (mass normalized to 1) corresponds to X' = [0 1; −k −b] X; eigenvalues are roots of λ^2 + b λ + k = 0, so discriminant b^2 − 4k determines behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If b^2 − 4k > 0: real distinct eigenvalues (overdamped), =0: repeated (critically damped), <0: complex eigenvalues (underdamped → oscillatory). For b=0, k>0 one gets pure imaginary eigenvalues (center → periodic motion). Describe motion for given initial conditions using the appropriate general solution form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological conjugacy (dynamical equivalence) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Two linear systems X' = A X and X' = B X are (topologically) conjugate if there exists a homeomorphism h: R^2 → R^2 such that φ_B(t, h(X0)) = h(φ_A(t, X0)) for all t and initial X0 (h is continuous, bijective, with continuous inverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjugacy preserves qualitative long-term behavior (sinks, sources, saddles, centers up to orientation). Example in 1D: x' = λ1 x and x' = λ2 x with same sign λ's are conjugate via h(x)=sign(x)|x|^{λ2/λ1}. Note: require homeomorphism (not necessarily diffeomorphism), because differentiability would force equality of rates (eigenvalues). Conjugacy can be realized by linear change of coords when systems are similar (T^{-1} A T = B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace/determinant as invariants and bifurcation indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace T and determinant D are algebraic invariants that determine eigenvalue configuration; curves in (T,D)-plane correspond to one-parameter families and their intersection with special loci indicates bifurcations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crossing the parabola T^2−4D=0 changes real/complex nature of eigenvalues; crossing the T-axis or positive D-axis changes stability (sink↔source) or sign patterns; note many different matrices map to the same (T,D) point, so TD-plane gives qualitative but not full geometric info (rotation direction, number of eigenvectors in repeated case may differ).
